proposals.hypothesis: LiF is a very wide-gap, insulating fluoride with no reducible transition-metal or La/Zr-reactive cations. Its F- anion is oxidatively stable near 4 V vs Li and is chemically inert toward both LiCoO2 and LLZO. The earlier oxide and phosphate coatings (Li3PO4, Li2ZrO3, LiNbO3, LiAlO2) all reacted with LLZO to form La- and Zr-containing products with penalties of about 0.08 to 0.10 eV/atom. A fluoride with no oxide-forming cation may avoid that contact reaction and bring the penalty below the 0.05 eV/atom threshold.
proposals.motivation: All four prior oxide/phosphate coatings were non-acceptable (penalties 0.08-0.10 from LLZO contact reactions releasing La-containing phosphates, niobates, or zirconates, plus a high self-decomposition penalty for Li2ZrO3). Switching to a halide anion chemistry is the clearest family change that could remove the contact reaction pathway.

proposals.hypothesis: Li2O is a wide-gap, insulating, purely Li-O oxide with no transition-metal, Zr, Nb, Ti, or Al cations to undergo redox or form La-containing products. Because LLZO is already Li-rich, Li2O should be chemically close to the electrolyte and less likely to react with it to form La-containing phases. Its Li+ content also keeps it compatible with the Li-rich garnet interface.

proposal.hypothesis: Li3PO4 is a wide-gap (~5 eV) lithium phosphate that is electronically insulating and oxidatively stable near 4 V vs Li, so it should block electron transfer at the LiCoO2 interface. Its P-O network is chemically compatible with both oxide electrodes, and it is a well-studied LiCoO2 and garnet interlayer, so interfacial penalty should be low.

Li2ZrO3 is a wide-gap, insulating lithium zirconate that shares the Zr-O and Li-O chemistry of the LLZO electrolyte, so it should be less reactive toward LLZO than the Li3PO4 interlayer, which released La/Zr-containing phosphate and O2 at contact. It is also a known oxide cathode coating for LiCoO2 that is chemically stable near 4 V vs Li, so it may reduce the contact penalty below the 0.05 eV/atom threshold.

proposal.hypothesis: LiNbO3 is a wide-gap, insulating lithium niobate that is a well-established protective coating on LiCoO2. Its Nb5+ centers are less easily reduced than Ti or Zr, and its Li-O-Nb framework is a different chemistry from the Li3PO4 and Li2ZrO3 coatings tested so far. The aim is a lower LLZO contact penalty than Li3PO4 (0.099 eV/atom) while avoiding the high self-decomposition penalty seen for Li2ZrO3 (0.30 eV/atom).

A non-reducible Al3+ oxide is a different chemistry that might avoid these failures.

proposal.hypothesis: LiF is a very wide-gap, insulating fluoride with no reducible transition-metal or La/Zr-reactive cations. Its F- anion is oxidatively stable near 4 V vs Li and is chemically inert toward both LiCoO2 and LLZO. The earlier oxide and phosphate coatings (Li3PO4, Li2ZrO3, LiNbO3, LiAlO2) all reacted with LLZO to form La- and Zr-containing products with penalties of about 0.08 to 0.10 eV/atom. A fluoride with no oxide-forming cation may avoid that contact reaction and bring the penalty below the 0.05 eV/atom threshold.

Switching to a halide anion chemistry is the clearest family change that could remove the contact reaction pathway.
